title: How to Scale Leadership Across an Organization
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author critiques the traditional model of leadership development — one-off training sessions and workshops — as insufficient for actually changing behavior, since leaders revert to old habits once the session ends. The alternative proposed is an ongoing, peer-led conversation where leaders regularly discuss real challenges, share best practices, and debate how to apply lessons to their own culture, rather than passively absorbing expert lectures. The piece emphasizes that this dialogue should be led by the organization's own senior leaders, not outside consultants, and stresses vibrant back-and-forth over one-directional presentation. It concludes that sustaining this kind of never-ending conversation is difficult but is the only approach that reliably scales leadership capability across an enterprise.
points: One-time training sessions and workshops rarely sustain real leadership behavior change.
Scaling leadership requires an ongoing, recurring conversation among peers, not periodic events.
Best-practice discussions led by an organization's own senior leaders are more engaging than outside experts.
The goal is vibrant debate and discussion, not leaders talking at each other.
Sustaining a continual dialogue is hard, but the piece argues it's the only approach that truly scales.
quotes: The good news is that most leaders want to be better. The bad news is they don’t know how.
The Sage on the Stage and one-and-done training programs sound great, but as soon as they are over, leaders get back to work.
Learning how to lead, like virtually everything else, requires an ongoing conversation that never ends.
Best practice discussions, led by the organization’s own senior leaders, make the effort highly engaging and memorable.
Nothing matches leaders teaching leaders as long as we remember it is a continual conversation, not a presentation.
The discipline to sustain a never-ending conversation is something foreign to most leaders.
